subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Market Day: Computing Costs and Finding Combinations

tasks_in_class.description: Find costs for different quantities of fruits/vegetables; find what combinations sum to ₹163 (more than one possibility).
Lou and Daisy buy 3 kg bananas (₹165). Which of the currency options a–e can they use to pay?

time_bands.activity: Introduce the market price list from the chapter context. Pairs read the list together and discuss: if you buy 2 kg of tomatoes, how much does it cost? Establish the unit-rate reasoning before moving to larger quantities.

Let Us Do, p.97 ("Find costs for different quantities; find combinations summing to ₹163...."). Children work in pairs, listing combinations systematically. Invite two or three pairs to share different solutions, emphasising that more than one answer is valid.

Let Us Do, p.98 ("Which currency options can pay for 3 kg bananas at ₹165?"). Children check each option against ₹165 and mark it valid or not, explaining their reasoning to a partner. Bring the class together to confirm which options work and why.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for children who treat the open combination task as having a single correct answer; prompt them with 'Can you find another pair of items?' to build comfort with multiple solutions. A common error is forgetting to multiply the price per kilogram by the quantity before adding — encourage children to write the unit price × quantity step explicitly. Play-money notes and coins on the desk help children verify currency combinations concretely.

section_titles: A Strange Puzzle — Change from Oranges
periods.activity_title: Cost–Paid–Balance Tables and the Orange Change Puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Complete 9 Cost–Paid–Balance grids by finding the missing value in each row.
Find the balance (paid amount minus ₹42) for Krishna (₹50), Sudama (₹100), Mala (₹200), and Neela (₹500).

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the idea of cost, paid amount, and balance using one oral example: 'A mango costs ₹15; I pay ₹20 — what is my balance?' Establish that balance = paid − cost.

Let Us Do, p.98 ("Complete 9 Cost–Paid–Balance grids by finding the missing value...."). Children work individually. Circulate to check whether children are subtracting (when cost and paid are given) or adding up (when balance and cost are given). Discuss the two directions of reasoning together.

A Strange Puzzle!, p.99 ("Find balance for Krishna ₹50, Sudama ₹100, Mala ₹200, Neela ₹500...."). Read the rhyme together. Children compute each balance and record it. Pairs compare answers and check by adding balance back to ₹42.

periods.teacher_notes: In the Cost–Paid–Balance grid, children often confuse which column is missing and subtract in the wrong direction — ask 'Is the cost or the payment bigger?' to orient them. For the rhyming puzzle, the check step (balance + ₹42 = amount paid) builds a verification habit that will serve the subtraction-with-regrouping work ahead. Keep play money available for children who need to count up to find the balance.

periods.activity_title: Magic Triangle: Arranging Numbers for Target Side-Sums

tasks_in_class.description: Place numbers 1–6 in triangle nodes so that the sum on each side is 9. No numbers repeated.
Use same numbers 1–6 and arrange so that the sum on each side of the triangle is 10.
What other sums can you make with these 6 numbers? Can you make 12 on each side? Can you make 13?

time_bands.activity: Draw the triangle outline on the board (3 vertices, 3 midpoints). Hand out number cards 1–6 or ask children to write them on slips. Explain the rule: each side has 3 numbers, and all three side-sums must be equal. Try one placement together as a class.

Let Us Play, p.100 ("Place numbers 1–6 so each side sums to 9...."). Children work individually or in pairs, moving their number slips. Encourage systematic trial: try placing the largest number at a vertex first. Share one working arrangement on the board.

Let Us Play, p.100 ("Arrange numbers 1–6 so each side sums to 10...."). Children rearrange their slips. Ask: which numbers sit at vertices in the sum-9 arrangement? Do the vertex numbers change for sum-10? Let pairs discuss before sharing.

Let Us Play, p.100 ("What other sums are possible? Can you make 12? 13?..."). Children explore freely. Collect claims on the board and test them together — celebrate both successful and unsuccessful attempts as part of mathematical exploration.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often start by placing numbers randomly; prompt systematic thinking by asking 'What is the total of all six numbers?' (21) and noting that each number is counted once or twice depending on position. A common error is placing a number in two nodes at once — remind them each card is used exactly once. The exploration of which sums are impossible is mathematically rich: guide children to notice that not every target is achievable.
materials: Number cards or slips labelled 1–6 (one set per pair)
Triangle outline sheet or drawn on a slate

periods.activity_title: Blocks and Columns: Building Two-Digit Addition with Regrouping

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate the number of teachers going on the trip (24 + 28) before computing.
Estimate the number of children going on the trip (438 + 476) before computing.
38 + 16: estimate the money spent on pusaw, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.

time_bands.activity: Use Dienes blocks or drawn block diagrams on the board. Show 24 (2 ten-sticks, 4 units) and 28 (2 ten-sticks, 8 units) side by side. Ask children to estimate the total before touching the blocks. Add Up, p.101 ("Estimate teachers going on the trip: 24 + 28...."). Combine the units — count 12 ones, regroup 10 ones into 1 ten, record in H-T-O columns.

Add Up, p.102 ("Estimate children going on the trip: 438 + 476...."). Move to 3-digit blocks. Children draw their own block diagrams in exercise books, combining ones first, then tens, then hundreds, regrouping at each stage. Compare estimates to the computed answer.

Add Up, p.103 ("Estimate money spent on pusaw: 38 + 16; fill H-T-O boxes...."). Children work in the H-T-O frame in the textbook, writing each step. Pairs check each other's regrouping step. Bring class together to confirm that 14 ones = 1 ten + 4 ones.

periods.teacher_notes: The key conceptual move is that regrouping is an exchange, not a mechanical carry — emphasise 'ten ones become one ten' with the blocks before writing the algorithm. Children frequently add the carried digit to the wrong column; walk through the H-T-O headers aloud. Estimation before computing is part of the task, not an optional step — insist on a written estimate so children can later judge whether their algorithm answer is reasonable.
materials: Dienes blocks or token sets (ones, tens, hundreds)
H-T-O column frame (on board and in textbook)

periods.activity_title: Three-Digit Addition: From Estimation to Algorithm and Word Problems

tasks_in_class.description: 185 + 125: estimate the trip money, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.
Complete the Kalakshitij table: find total boys, total girls, total tabla players, and total singers.
Preeti's school has 423 children; cousin's school has 178 more. How many children study in Preeti's cousin's school?

homework.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 follow-up, p.105
homework.description: 15 more girls join to play tabla. How many girls play tabla now?

time_bands.activity: Add Up, p.104 ("Estimate trip money: 185 + 125; fill H-T-O boxes...."). Children estimate first (round each to the nearest ten or hundred), then compute step by step in the H-T-O frame, regrouping tens into hundreds where needed.

Let Us Do Q1, p.105 ("Complete Kalakshitij table: total boys, girls, tabla players, singers...."). Children work through the table independently, adding along rows and columns. Circulate and prompt: 'Which two numbers are you adding? Are the ones digits going to regroup?'
Let Us Do Q2, p.105 ("Add by aligning in columns: 32+47, 654+95, 286+123...."). Children set up each pair in H-T-O columns in their exercise books and compute, checking their alignment before adding.

Let Us Do Q3, p.105 ("Preeti's school: 423; cousin's school has 178 more — how many?..."). Children write and solve the addition statement. One child explains the solution to the class. The follow-up (15 more girls join tabla) is set as homework for consolidation.

periods.teacher_notes: Misalignment of digits is the most frequent error in column addition — reinforce the habit of drawing H, T, O headers before writing numbers. The table task (Q1) is a good moment to discuss that addition is the same operation whether applied to rows or columns. Where children finish early, encourage them to verify their Q2 answers by swapping addends and re-adding.

periods.activity_title: Regrouping to Subtract: Two- and Three-Digit Differences

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate the difference: how many more children bought Pusaw than fruit plates (83 − 46)?
Estimate how many children are waiting to visit the Living Roots Bridge (438 − 215).
Ram Chacha: 527 mangoes this year, 264 last year. Estimate then find how many more mangoes this year; use/draw tokens.

time_bands.activity: Subtract It, p.106 ("Estimate: how many more bought Pusaw than fruit plates — 83 − 46?..."). Model with Dienes blocks: lay out 8 ten-sticks and 3 units. Ask: can we take 6 units from 3? Demonstrate breaking one ten into 10 units, then subtracting. Children estimate first, then compute in H-T-O.

Subtract It, p.106 ("Estimate children waiting at the Living Roots Bridge: 438 − 215..."). Children draw block diagrams showing hundreds, tens, and ones, subtracting column by column starting from ones. Pairs compare their steps and results.

Let Us Solve, p.108 ("Ram Chacha's mangoes: 527 − 264; estimate then use/draw tokens...."). Children draw token representations, regroup where needed, and record the algorithm. Ask one child to explain the regrouping step aloud using 'regroup' (not 'borrow').

periods.teacher_notes: Children need to hear and use the word 'regroup' consistently — it means exchanging 1 ten for 10 ones, not borrowing something to be returned. A common error is subtracting the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position (e.g. writing 83 − 46 as 43 instead of 37); the block model makes this error visible immediately. Encourage children to always estimate before computing so they can catch large errors in their answer.
materials: H-T-O column frame (on board and in textbook)

periods.activity_title: Subtraction Drill: Regrouping Across Tens and Hundreds

tasks_in_class.description: Ranganna made 639 dolls, sold 531. Estimate then find how many dolls are left; use/draw tokens.
Subtract by aligning in columns: (a) 83−29 (b) 345−123 (c) 763−437 (d) 803−350 (e) 900−328.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q4, p.108 ("Ranganna's dolls: 639 − 531; estimate then draw tokens...."). Children write an estimate, draw the token model, and carry out the algorithm. Highlight that 639 − 531 requires no regrouping in the ones place — contrast with the previous examples to reinforce that regrouping is needed only when the ones digit being subtracted is larger.

Let Us Solve Q5, p.109 ("Subtract in columns: 83−29, 345−123, 763−437, 803−350, 900−328..."). Children set up each subtraction in H-T-O columns. Circulate: pause the class briefly after (c) to discuss how to regroup from the hundreds place when the tens digit is already 0, using 803 − 350 or 900 − 328 as the class example.

periods.teacher_notes: The case 900 − 328 is the most demanding because regrouping must happen twice — from hundreds to tens and then from tens to ones. Draw the block exchange on the board before children attempt it independently. A common error is writing a 0 in the tens of the answer without regrouping from hundreds; the block diagram makes the exchange concrete.

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
periods.activity_title: Library and Train: Multi-Step Word Problems in Addition and Subtraction

tasks_in_class.description: Rami read Panchatantra Tales (236 pages); Kesu read Akbar Birbal, Karadi Tales, and Blue Umbrella. Who read more? How many more pages?
Sumi has read 23 pages of Adventures of Feluda (128 pages). How many more pages are left?
Jaggu reads all 6 books (total pages). He has finished Swami and Friends, Akbar Birbal, and 50 pages of Feluda. How many pages left?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Solve a and b, p.111
tasks_in_class.description: Column addition and subtraction: (a) 452+89 (b) 641−273.

time_bands.activity: Display the library book list from p.110 on the board. Read through the book titles and page counts together. Ask children: 'To answer Q1a, do you add or subtract? How do you know?' Establish the plan before computing.

Let Us Solve Q1a, p.110 ("Rami vs. Kesu: who read more pages?...") and Q1b, p.110 ("Pages left in Adventures of Feluda..."). Children work through both, writing their number sentence and computation. Pairs share and check Q1b by adding 23 and their answer to confirm they get 128.

Let Us Solve Q1c, p.110 ("Jaggu reads all 6 books; pages left after 3 books and 50 pages of Feluda..."). Children must first find the grand total, then subtract the pages already read. Circulate and ask: 'What is the first step? What is the second?'
Let Us Solve a and b, p.111 ("452+89; 641−273...."). Children work in columns independently and verify by re-reading the H-T-O steps. Quick class check of answers before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Multi-step problems are demanding because children must decide the operation sequence before computing — Q1c requires two steps (total pages, then subtract). Encourage children to write their plan in words before writing any numbers. A common error is computing the right operations in the wrong order; ask 'What do you need to know first?' to prompt sequencing.
materials: Library book list (p.110, displayed on board)

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
periods.activity_title: Train Journey, Quick Strategies, and Making Your Own Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Train problem: how many passengers on the train when it leaves Dadri (after boarding 158, alighting 23, boarding 67, alighting 75 at stops)?
Find the number of people who got off the train at Aligarh (final destination).
Find quick ways to solve: 326+25, 410−12, 675+5, 204−10, 811+99, 945−19 using strategies from Grade 3.
Find two numbers whose sum is 856 and two numbers whose difference is 563; then make your own word problems with these numbers.

homework.description: Were there more people on the train in New Delhi or in Aligarh? How much more/less?
How many people travelled altogether by the train?

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q2a–b, p.111 ("Train journey: passengers at each stop; how many at Dadri? Who got off at Aligarh?..."). Draw a simple route diagram on the board (stations as stops, arrows for board/alight). Children track the running total stop by stop, recording each addition or subtraction.

Let Us Solve c, p.111 ("Quick strategies: 326+25, 410−12, 675+5, 204−10, 811+99, 945−19..."). Show the speech-bubble model from the textbook. Children write their mental strategy for each, e.g. 'Add 30 then subtract 5' for +25. Pairs share strategies and decide which is quickest.

Let Us Solve e, p.112 ("Find pairs summing to 856 and differing by 563; write your own word problems..."). Children first find the number pairs, then compose a word problem context for each. Two children read their word problems aloud. Remaining train sub-questions (Q2c, Q2d) are set as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The train problem is the chapter's most sustained multi-step context; a route diagram on the board dramatically reduces confusion about which direction (board or alight) each action goes. For the quick-strategies task, the goal is flexible thinking — there is no single correct method, and celebrating different valid strategies builds confidence. The word-problem composition task is open: any pair of numbers whose sum is 856 is acceptable.

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
periods.activity_title: Number Pair Hunt and Missing Digits: Strategic Reasoning

tasks_in_class.description: How many number pairs (adjacent vertically or horizontally) are there in the 4×4 grid?
Find the number pair in the grid whose sum is the greatest.
Find the number pair in the grid whose difference is the greatest.
Fill the missing digits in 3 addition puzzles and 3 subtraction puzzles to make each sum correct.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve d, p.111 ("Align in columns: 38+943, 465+305, 435+462, 764−657, 518−209, 879−53..."). Children work independently with H-T-O headers. Spot-check alignment and regrouping as they work.

Number Pair Hunt, p.112–113 ("Count adjacent pairs; find pair with greatest sum; find pair with greatest difference..."). Children first count all valid adjacent pairs (Q at p.112), then hunt for the greatest-sum pair and the greatest-difference pair. Pairs record their candidates and compute to verify.

The Missing Digits, p.113 ("Fill missing digits in 3 addition and 3 subtraction puzzles...."). Children work backwards: for addition, ask 'What digit makes the ones column correct?'; for subtraction, ask 'What must have been regrouped?' Share solutions and verify by computing the completed sum.

periods.teacher_notes: The Number Pair Hunt rewards a systematic search — children who scan randomly often miss pairs. Prompt them to go row by row (horizontal pairs) then column by column (vertical pairs) to count all valid pairs before hunting for the greatest. Missing-digit puzzles are solved by reverse reasoning, not guessing; model the first puzzle with the class, asking aloud 'If the ones digits sum to this, what is the missing digit?' Additional practice for Q2 (smallest sum) and Q4 (smallest difference) is available at Number Pair Hunt Q2 and Q4, p.113.
materials: 4×4 number grid (p.112, or copied on board)

section_titles: Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill
periods.activity_title: Final Drill: Mixed Addition and Subtraction with Multiple Regroupings

time_bands.activity: Set the context: this is a full-range drill covering 2- and 3-digit addition and subtraction including cases with multiple regroupings. Ask children to predict which additions will require regrouping and which will not, by looking at the digits — building estimation and scanning habits before computing.

Let Us Do Q1, p.114 ("Add: 23+489, 105+295, 630+56, 35+99, 409+387, 67+76, 580+207, 333+666, 826+268..."). Children work through all nine additions in H-T-O columns. Circulate and flag 826+268 as the case needing double regrouping — support children who get stuck there with a brief block-exchange reminder.

Let Us Do Q2, p.114 ("Subtract: 300−45, 962−268, 706−209, 842−387, 674−76, 754−409, 403−245, 600−384, 546−538..."). Children work through all nine subtractions. Pause the class briefly when most reach 600−384 or 403−245 to discuss regrouping from a zero tens digit.

Children self-check three chosen answers by reversing the operation (add back to verify subtraction; subtract to verify addition). Invite one child to share a case where the reverse check caught an error.

periods.teacher_notes: The cases 826+268 (addition with double carry) and 600−384 or 706−209 (subtraction through a zero) are the hardest in this drill — be ready to draw the block-exchange diagram for any child who stalls. The self-check step at the end builds a verification habit: subtraction answer + subtrahend = minuend is a method children can always apply independently. Encourage children to estimate the magnitude of each answer before computing to catch unreasonable results.

items.prompt: Apples cost ₹40 per kg and oranges cost ₹30 per kg. Meena wants to spend exactly ₹100 on fruits. Which of the following could she buy?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the price per kilogram by the quantity for each fruit, then add the two amounts and check whether the total equals ₹100.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have added 40+30 and stopped, or confused the quantities — 2 kg apples + 1 kg oranges = ₹80+₹30 = ₹110, not ₹100.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have checked only one fruit type — 3 kg apples = ₹120, not ₹100.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have added without multiplying — 2 kg apples + 2 kg oranges = ₹80+₹60 = ₹140, not ₹100.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a price table and ask them to fill cost = price × kg before adding; stretch: ask them to find a second valid combination.

exercise.description: Find costs for different quantities of fruits/vegetables; find what combinations sum to ₹163 (more than one possibility).

items.prompt: Tomatoes cost ₹25 per kg. Ravi wants to buy 3 kg of tomatoes and pays with a ₹100 note. Which statement about his change is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: He cannot pay with ₹100 because it is not enough

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the total cost by multiplying the price by 3, then subtract from ₹100 to find the balance.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have computed ₹100 − ₹25 = ₹75 without first finding the total cost of 3 kg.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have estimated incorrectly or confused which is larger — ₹100 is greater than ₹75.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have halved ₹100 without any connection to the cost calculation.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first write ₹25 × 3 = ? before thinking about the change; stretch: ask what change they would receive if they paid with a ₹500 note.

exercise.description: Lou and Daisy buy 3 kg bananas (₹165). Which of the currency options a–e can they use to pay?

items.prompt: In a Magic Triangle, the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 are placed in six circles — one at each corner and one on each side — so that every side adds up to the same total. Arjun places 6, 1, 2 along one side and gets a side sum of 9. He says the side sum of 13 is impossible using these six numbers. Is Arjun right? Write 'Yes' or 'No' and explain your thinking in one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Arjun is right. A side sum of 13 is impossible because the three corner numbers would need to be very large, and with only the numbers 1–6 available the highest achievable side sum is 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Consider what the largest possible three numbers along one side can be from the set 1–6 and check whether their sum can reach 13.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to try placing 4, 5, 6 along one side and compute the sum to see the maximum; stretch: ask what the smallest possible side sum is and explain why.

exercise.description: What other sums can you make with these 6 numbers? Can you make 12 on each side? Can you make 13?

items.prompt: Before adding 47 + 36, Priya estimates the answer by rounding each number to the nearest ten. What is her estimate?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 47 rounds to 50; 36 rounds to 40; estimate = 50 + 40 = 90. Wait — re-check: 47 rounds to 50, 36 rounds to 40, so 50+40=90. Recheck: the correct answer is 90.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round 47 to 50 and 36 to 40, then add the rounded numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have rounded both numbers down (40 + 30 = 70), not to the nearest ten.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have rounded one number correctly and the other incorrectly (e.g., 40 + 40 = 80).
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student computed the exact answer (83) without estimating, showing they did not round first.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a number line showing tens (30, 40, 50, 60) and ask which ten 47 is nearest to; stretch: ask them to judge whether the exact answer will be above or below the estimate and why.

exercise.description: Estimate the number of teachers going on the trip (24 + 28) before computing.

items.prompt: Tara wants to estimate 92 − 47 before computing. She rounds each number to the nearest ten. What is her estimate?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 92 rounds to 90; 47 rounds to 50; estimate = 90 − 50 = 40. Re-check: 90 − 50 = 40. The correct answer is 40, not 50.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round 92 to 90 and 47 to 50, then subtract the rounded numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have rounded 47 to 40 and computed 90 − 40 = 50, rounding 47 down rather than up.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have computed the exact answer (45) rather than estimating with rounded numbers.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have added instead of subtracting after rounding, or used a different rounding.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the student a tens number line and ask them to mark 92 and 47, then read off the nearest tens; stretch: ask them to say whether the exact answer will be greater or less than the estimate and justify.

exercise.description: Estimate the difference: how many more children bought Pusaw than fruit plates (83 − 46)?

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Sneha wants to add 298 + 5 quickly without writing a column sum. Describe a quick mental strategy she could use and write the answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Strategy: add 2 to 298 to make 300, then add the remaining 3 to get 303. Answer: 303.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Break 5 into 2 + 3; add 2 to 298 to reach the round number 300, then add 3 more.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first find what number makes 298 into 300, then think about what is left from 5; stretch: ask them to apply a similar strategy to 397 + 8.

exercise.description: Find quick ways to solve: 326+25, 410−12, 675+5, 204−10, 811+99, 945−19 using strategies from Grade 3.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Write two different numbers whose sum is 740. Then write a short word problem (one or two sentences) that uses these two numbers and the operation of addition.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two numbers that add to 740 are correct (e.g., 400 and 340, or 500 and 240). The word problem should involve adding those two numbers to get 740.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose any number less than 740, subtract it from 740 to find the second number, then write a real-life situation where the two amounts combine.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student one of the numbers (say 300) and ask them to find the other by computing 740 − 300; stretch: ask them to write a second word problem using subtraction with the same pair of numbers.

exercise.description: Find two numbers whose sum is 856 and two numbers whose difference is 563; then make your own word problems with these numbers.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: In a Missing Digits addition puzzle, the ones column shows: 7 + ☐ = 13. What is the missing digit? What do you carry to the tens column?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Missing digit is 6 (because 7 + 6 = 13). Write 3 in the ones place and carry 1 to the tens column.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Think: what number added to 7 gives 13? The answer is 6; the digit 3 stays in ones and 1 ten is carried.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count up from 7 on their fingers until they reach 13 and count how many fingers they raised; stretch: give them a two-column missing-digit puzzle where both the ones and tens digits are missing.

exercise.description: Fill the missing digits in 3 addition puzzles and 3 subtraction puzzles to make each sum correct.

items.prompt: Add the following numbers by writing them in H-T-O columns and regrouping where needed: 367 + 84.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Ones: 7 + 4 = 11; write 1, carry 1 ten. Tens: 6 + 8 + 1 = 15; write 5, carry 1 hundred. Hundreds: 3 + 1 = 4. Answer: 451.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a blank H-T-O grid and ask them to write each digit in its correct column before adding; stretch: ask them to add a third number: 367 + 84 + 15.

items.prompt: Subtract by aligning in H-T-O columns and regrouping where needed: 504 − 268.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Ones: cannot take 8 from 4; regroup 1 ten from the tens place — but tens digit is 0, so regroup 1 hundred to get 10 tens, then regroup 1 ten to get 10 ones; ones: 14 − 8 = 6; tens: 9 − 6 = 3; hundreds: 4 − 2 = 2. Answer: 236.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the student block diagrams where a hundred is broken into 10 tens and then a ten into 10 ones; stretch: ask them to verify by adding 268 + 236 and checking they get 504.

exercise.description: Subtract by aligning in columns: (a) 83−29 (b) 345−123 (c) 763−437 (d) 803−350 (e) 900−328.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Ones: 6 + 8 = 14; write 4, carry 1. Tens: 2 + 6 + 1 = 9. Hundreds: 8 + 2 = 10; write 0, carry 1. Thousands: 1. Answer: 1094.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first add the ones, write the carry, then the tens, step by step using a labelled H-T-O column grid with a Th column added; stretch: ask them to find a different pair of 3-digit numbers that also add to 1094.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill
items.prompt: Subtract: 600 − 384.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Ones: cannot take 4 from 0; tens digit is 0 too, so regroup 1 hundred into 10 tens, then 1 ten into 10 ones: ones 10 − 4 = 6; tens 9 − 8 = 1; hundreds 5 − 3 = 2. Answer: 216.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 6 hundred-blocks and exchange one for 10 ten-blocks, then one ten-block for 10 one-blocks before subtracting; stretch: ask the student to verify by adding 384 + 216 and checking they get 600.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper sells grapes for ₹60 per kg. A customer buys 2 kg of grapes and pays with a ₹200 note. How much change does the shopkeeper return?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply price per kilogram by the number of kilograms to find cost, then subtract cost from the amount paid.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a Cost–Paid–Balance table and ask the student to fill each column step by step; stretch: ask what change would be returned if the customer had paid with two ₹100 notes instead.

exercise.description: Complete 9 Cost–Paid–Balance grids by finding the missing value in each row.

items.section_title: A Strange Puzzle — Change from Oranges
items.prompt: Two apples cost ₹36 altogether. Raj pays for them with a ₹200 note. How much change does he receive?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the cost (₹36) from the amount paid (₹200), regrouping from the hundreds as needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count up from ₹36 to ₹200 on a number line, adding tens and hundreds; stretch: ask how much change Raj would receive if he had paid with a ₹500 note.

exercise.description: Find the balance (paid amount minus ₹42) for Krishna (₹50), Sudama (₹100), Mala (₹200), and Neela (₹500).

items.prompt: A school library has 265 Hindi books and 148 English books. How many books are there altogether?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add ones (5 + 8 = 13; write 3, carry 1), then tens (6 + 4 + 1 = 11; write 1, carry 1), then hundreds (2 + 1 + 1 = 4). Answer: 413.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw Dienes blocks for 265 and 148 and combine them column by column; stretch: ask how many more books are needed to reach a total of 500.

exercise.description: 185 + 125: estimate the trip money, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.

items.prompt: A garden has 356 rose plants. A neighbouring garden has 219 more rose plants than the first garden. How many rose plants are in the neighbouring garden?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the two numbers in H-T-O columns: ones 6 + 9 = 15 (write 5, carry 1); tens 5 + 1 + 1 = 7; hundreds 3 + 2 = 5. Answer: 575.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write 356 + 219 in H-T-O columns before computing; stretch: ask what the total number of rose plants in both gardens is.

exercise.description: Preeti's school has 423 children; cousin's school has 178 more. How many children study in Preeti's cousin's school?

items.prompt: A farmer harvested 743 coconuts this season and 389 coconuts last season. How many more coconuts did the farmer harvest this season?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Ones: 3 < 9, regroup; 13 − 9 = 4. Tens: 3 < 8 (after regroup tens become 3), regroup; 13 − 8 = 5. Hundreds: 6 − 3 = 3. Answer: 354.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw token blocks for 743 and exchange as needed before subtracting; stretch: ask them to verify by adding 389 + 354 and checking the total.

exercise.description: Ram Chacha: 527 mangoes this year, 264 last year. Estimate then find how many more mangoes this year; use/draw tokens.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: A community library has these books: Fiction — 312 pages, Poetry — 85 pages, Science — 143 pages. Tara reads the Fiction book and the Poetry book. Kesu reads the Science book and the Fiction book. Who reads more pages, and by how many?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Tara: 312 + 85 = 397 pages. Kesu: 143 + 312 = 455 pages. Kesu reads more by 455 − 397 = 58 pages.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add each reader's pages separately, then subtract the smaller total from the larger to find the difference.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a two-row table (Tara's books | Kesu's books) to fill in before adding; stretch: ask how many total pages all three books have together.

exercise.description: Rami read Panchatantra Tales (236 pages); Kesu read Akbar Birbal, Karadi Tales, and Blue Umbrella. Who read more? How many more pages?

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Priya has a storybook with 245 pages. She has read 78 pages of Chapter 1 and 64 pages of Chapter 2. How many pages of the book are still left to read?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: First add the pages already read (78 + 64 = 142), then subtract from the total (245 − 142 = 103).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first write 'pages read so far = ?' and compute that before attempting the subtraction; stretch: ask how many more pages Priya needs to read each day to finish the book in exactly 5 equal portions.

exercise.description: Jaggu reads all 6 books (total pages). He has finished Swami and Friends, Akbar Birbal, and 50 pages of Feluda. How many pages left?

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: A train starts with 0 passengers. At Stop 1, 125 people board. At Stop 2, 48 people get off and 73 people board. How many passengers are on the train after Stop 2?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track the running total at each stop: add boarders and subtract those who alight, step by step.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a simple diagram with Stop 1 and Stop 2 boxes and arrows for board/alight, filling each box with the running total; stretch: ask what would happen if 90 more people boarded at a Stop 3, and whether the total would cross 250.

exercise.description: Train problem: how many passengers on the train when it leaves Dadri (after boarding 158, alighting 23, boarding 67, alighting 75 at stops)?
